body.text: The 18th BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa) Summit, held in New Delhi between September 12 and 13, 2026, was expected by many to mark the bloc’s transition from rhetoric to a concrete challenge to the dollar. It did not. The New Delhi Declaration committed members to expanding local-currency trade and interoperable payment systems, including BRICS Pay, but stopped well short of proposing a common currency.

The joint statement of BRICS finance ministers and central bank governors ahead of the summit was similarly cautious. That caution reflects a deeper reality shaping BRICS’s monetary ambitions since 2022: the freezing of hundreds of billions of dollars in Russian sovereign reserves, and the exclusion of Russian banks from much of the Western financial system, showed governments across the Global South that dollar reserves are not merely financial assets but can also become instruments of geopolitical leverage. The political grievance behind de-dollarisation is real. The economic case for a wholesale monetary rupture is considerably weaker.

Commentary on BRICS oscillates between predictions of the dollar’s imminent collapse and dismissive Western complacency. The more consequential reality lies between the two. BRICS is seeking to reduce its members’ exposure to a system in which access to the dominant currency can carry geopolitical consequences. Reducing dependence on the dollar, however, is not the same as replacing it. The bloc’s alternative channels for trade, payments and development finance remain constrained by trade imbalances, convertibility limits, and shallow financial markets. The New Delhi summit did little to resolve these constraints, whatever the ambition of its payment-system announcements.

The most persistent error in the BRICS debate is conflating a transaction currency with a reserve currency. Bilateral trade settled in national currencies, i.e., rupees, roubles or yuan, can reduce dollar exposure in particular transactions and offer some insulation from sanctions. It does not, by itself, create a self-sustaining international monetary system.

A reserve currency requires deep, liquid financial markets, broad convertibility, and a large supply of safe assets that foreign governments can hold. The Triffin dilemma captures part of the problem: a currency serving as the world’s principal liquidity asset must be supplied abroad on a sustained basis, creating pressures that most BRICS members cannot or will not absorb. China illustrates this sharply. It is the bloc’s economic centre of gravity, yet also runs a structural surplus. The yuan can expand as a settlement currency without becoming an equally attractive reserve asset, given Beijing’s restrictions on capital-account convertibility.

The post-2022 India-Russia oil trade makes the problem concrete. As trade expanded and payments moved outside the dollar, Russian exporters accumulated rupee balances in Indian banks that, according to Reuters reporting, peaked at as much as $39 billion. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov acknowledged this in 2023, telling reporters in Goa that “this is a problem” and that the rupees needed to be converted before Moscow could use them. India’s large trade deficit with Russia limited Moscow’s ability to recycle the balances through imports, while capital-account restrictions constrained their wider use. Removing the dollar from a transaction does not remove the need for a mechanism to settle the resulting claims. Moscow’s subsequent shift towards the yuan and the UAE dirham in some deals changed the settlement currency; it did not solve the underlying problem. Nor does BRICS Pay resolve it, since interoperable payment systems cannot, by themselves, create convertibility or investable assets.

The same constraint shapes institutions created as alternatives to Western-dominated development finance. The New Development Bank (NDB) and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement were designed to give emerging economies greater institutional autonomy. But institutional independence does not mean operating outside the global financial system.

The NDB needs access to international capital markets to expand lending beyond member subscriptions, making it sensitive to investor perceptions and credit assessments. Days after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the NDB announced that it had “put new transactions in Russia on hold” amid “unfolding uncertainties and restrictions”, reflecting constraints imposed by its own financial position and its access to international capital markets. A founding member found that the bank it had helped create could not continue transactions with it once geopolitical restrictions collided with its financial obligations. This does not make the NDB irrelevant; it marks the boundary between institutional diversification and genuine financial independence.

This places New Delhi at the centre of a delicate calculation, one visible in its summit diplomacy. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar has repeatedly said there is “no proposal to have a BRICS currency” and that the grouping has “no interest in weakening the US dollar at all”, a position India maintained even while hosting a summit built around expanding non-dollar payment infrastructure. India’s relationship with China remains marked by substantial trade asymmetry, while its wider interests remain deeply connected with the US, Europe, and the Gulf. A BRICS currency built around a single member’s financial infrastructure could raise concentration concerns that New Delhi has no interest in inviting.

India’s approach has therefore been incremental: greater international use of the rupee, cross-border digital payment links and bilateral mechanisms that reduce dollar use in selected transactions, while avoiding a single BRICS currency or an antagonistic bloc. Bilateral arrangements can reduce specific vulnerabilities, but they cannot, by themselves, generate the scale, liquidity, and network effects required for a genuinely diversified monetary system.

BRICS’s members do not, in any case, form a unified political economy. They include commodity exporters, manufacturers, energy producers, and services economies whose financial systems and capital controls diverge sharply, a divergence Jaishankar has himself acknowledged, noting that BRICS members hold “very diverse positions” on the currency question.

The New Delhi summit did not produce a sudden monetary revolution, and BRICS does not need one to alter the existing system. Bilateral trade may increasingly be settled in national currencies; central banks may diversify reserves; payment systems such as BRICS Pay may develop outside Western channels. None of this, individually, displaces the dollar. Collectively, it can reduce the number of transactions for which the dollar is indispensable.

The New Delhi Declaration will likely be read, in time, less as a step towards replacing the dollar than as confirmation that the dollar’s dominance is becoming progressively less exclusive. That may be the more consequential form of de-dollarisation: not a new order, but enough alternatives to make dependence on the old one less automatic. The dollar remained the summit’s unstated centre of gravity even as its host built systems designed to need it less.
